This depends a lot on what kind of games you're playing. Many amazing games like Dwarf Fortress, Factorio or most of the Grand Strategy stuff released by Paradox care a lot more about CPU than graphics- or physics-oriented games like Rocket League or the latest Call of Duty.

These CPU-intensive games exist, and they've started to break out of being a niche market. No matter how much game "journalists" hate to make the effort required to familiarize themselves with genres that require more than twitch reflex and good depth perception.

I don't see the point of this video. Its obvious going to result in some highly processor dependent games running well below the GPU's potentiality with the games less dependent on processor run reasonably well. Its a bit of a given, I've seen it myself with Thief in DX11 and Mantle, my 280x struggled to play the game with my old Q6600 CPU working its little heart out but under Mantle frame rates doubled with considerably less CPU activity overall.

Preform the same test with lets say Doom in OpenGL and then in Vulkan. That will be extremely interesting because Vulkan, with its Mantle roots isn't designed to let to unlock extra performance on GPU's it was designed to free AMD cards from CPU bound scenarios which even on a Nvidia GPU should have a substantial impact on performance.
The point is to show people that really old hardware can still do a lot. Will it do everything? No. Will it do most of what people want at a bargain basement price? Yes.

Obviously this is /v/gaming so we're mainly just worried about game performance here, but I just wanted to mention that outside of gaming there are many reasons why CPU still matters. Try transcoding 1080p video on the fly and even some brand new lower end CPUs will choke. I seem to remember even higher end i7s having trouble with it a few generations back.

I have two first generation i7s (920s), they have no problems transcoding 1080p on the fly. They also have no problems playing any modern game, even those which are considered CPU heavy. You're vastly overestimating how much CPU transcoding needs.

I always had problems with big 1080p bluray rips. It's possible that the HDD was the bottleneck though. At some point I moved the transcoding directory to RAM (mounted as tmpfs) and that very well could've been what made the difference. I will say that plex uses a good portion of my overclocked 6700k (4.7GHz) when I turn transcoding up to "make my CPU hurt".

I think it has a lot to do with your implementation for transcoding, though I think you could be right about drive speed particularly if your input files are very large. I moved to SSDs and SSHDs a while ago and never looked back. If you haven't done this yet, do it. You won't believe how much of a difference it makes to everything.

If you're trying to force the entire job on to one core you'll probably have problems. Plex has changed over the years, so they may have improved multi-core performance. Where you might run in to issues is transcoding several streams at the same time. Generally speaking I'm only ever performing a single Plex transcode, so I don't know how it'd fare with multiple jobs.

My 920s are not overclocked, and they run at 2.66ghz. To this day I haven't encountered anything in my own use cases that they can't do.
Considering I can't run ArmA at anything above 45fps on an i5, but it runs over 60 on an i7, I think it matters more to me than this video thinks.
Totally depends on the game. Most games, CPU doesn't matter much.
Most games don't take advantage of hyperthreading or multiple cores.

You need to consider the cost to performance ratio though. The OP isn't saying "this is all you'll ever need", he's intimating that it works better than you might think it does. When you consider that this is a $25 CPU the benefits of building a passable gaming system with one become more obvious. By saving on the CPU and the mainboard, you have more money to put in to video hardware which is arguably more important for many modern games.

People get in to the mindset with PCs that they must have the most modern hardware to get by, but often this isn't the case. Many performance characteristics of PCs have plateaued, and it's more about energy/heat efficiency and parallel processing now which have far less impact on most titles.
Even a dual core would be enough for pretty much everything. It's not about cpu power now a days. It's all about the graphics card and ram.
